title: AI doesn't need to know your race to discriminate against you
full_text:
Technology More data promises sharper predictions and a competitive edge. But the same systems can make bias harder to see and easier to reproduce.
Artificial intelligence is being promoted as a means of making better decisions.
Banks use algorithms to assess loan applications. Employers screen candidates using data. Online platforms decide which advertisements people see. Insurers use increasingly detailed information to assess risk and set premiums.
The attraction is obvious. More data promises sharper predictions and a competitive edge.
But the same systems can make discrimination harder to see - and easier to reproduce at scale.
Recent media coverage of Australian insurance pricing has brought this issue into public view. It has raised questions about the unconventional information that may influence premiums, where that information comes from, and whether it can disadvantage particular communities.
The issue is not limited to insurance. Similar concerns arise in lending, employment, advertising, healthcare and government services.
The central problem is not simply whether an organisation directly uses race, religion, gender or another protected characteristic when making decisions. It is also a question of whether apparently neutral information acts as a proxy for one of those characteristics.
It might seem that discrimination can be avoided by excluding protected characteristics from a dataset.
This idea is sometimes called "fairness through unawareness". If a model does not know someone's race or religion, how can it discriminate?
The answer is that it may infer this information indirectly.
Postcodes can reflect the ethnic or racial composition of neighbourhoods. Names, language, education, occupation, purchasing patterns, eating habits and online behaviour may all contain information about a person's background.
A model does not need to be told that someone belongs to a particular group. It may identify other characteristics closely associated with group membership and use them in making its decision.
The risk increases as organisations collect more information. A variable may appear harmless on its own. Combined with hundreds of other variables, it may help reproduce patterns of disadvantage that the organisation never intended to use.
Insurance illustrates the difficulty. People pay different premiums because insurers assess their expected risk. Actuaries are familiar with the principle that people with the same level of risk should, in general, pay the same price.
But a variable can be predictive without being a legitimate basis for pricing. Statistical association alone does not show that a factor is relevant to the risk being insured, fair to customers or appropriate to use.
Australian anti-discrimination law treats race differently from other protected attributes. In specified circumstances, the Sex Discrimination Act, Age Discrimination Act and Disability Discrimination Act allow insurers to rely on actuarial or statistical data when setting premiums. The Racial Discrimination Act does not contain an equivalent exemption.
Guidance from the Australian Human Rights Commission and Actuaries Institute makes clear that removing protected attributes from a dataset does not, of itself, eliminate the risk of discrimination. Other variables may still act as proxies for those attributes.
The challenge is not limited to information collected directly by an organisation.
Third-party data companies can combine public and commercial information and package it for businesses.
Some products classify neighbourhoods according to characteristics such as household composition, education, court judgments and affluence. Other providers analyse browsing activity, social media behaviour, purchasing patterns and other digital traces.
Australia's Privacy Act regulates how personal information is collected, used and disclosed. In many circumstances, organisations need consent or another permitted legal basis.
To reduce privacy risks, information shared with businesses is therefore often aggregated or de-identified. That does not make every concern disappear.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has warned that de-identified information may present re-identification risks when datasets are combined. It has also raised concerns about consumers being categorised and targeted according to shared characteristics.
The issue is not simply how data is obtained, but what can be inferred from it and how those inferences affect people.
Predictive accuracy is not enough.
The answer is not to reject artificial intelligence or every unconventional source of data. Better prediction can bring real benefits.
But predictive accuracy cannot be the only test.
Organisations should ask whether a variable is truly relevant to the decision, whether its use is consistent with legal and community expectations, and whether it produces unfair outcomes. They should test their models regularly and be prepared to remove variables that cannot be properly justified.
This is a responsibility shared by boards, regulators, actuaries, data scientists and other professionals involved in automated decision-making.
An algorithm finding a pattern is not, by itself, a reason to use it. The real question is whether that pattern gives an organisation a fair basis for deciding what someone pays, whether they get a job or how they are treated.
Fei Huang is associate professor of risk and actuarial studies at University of NSW Business School and an expert in fair insurance pricing and responsible AI.
